Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Apex Energy First Quarter 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. [Operator Instructions] Please note this event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Alex Rivera, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera: Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Apex Energy's first quarter 2024 earnings call. Joining me on the call today are John Hargrove, Chief Executive Officer; Sarah Ellis, Chief Financial Officer; Mike Thompson, Chief Operating Officer; and Elena Vasquez, VP of Exploration.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we make today may be forward-looking. These statements are based on current expectations and assumptions and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to our SEC filings for a more detailed discussion of these risks.

I will now turn the call over to John Hargrove.

John Hargrove: Thank you, Alex, and good morning, everyone. Apex Energy delivered solid results in the first quarter, driven by strong operational performance and favorable commodity prices. We achieved robust production growth across our key basins. I'm particularly pleased with our progress on midstream throughput and infrastructure builds. We remain deeply committed to advancing our ESG initiatives, especially emissions reductions. Further, we maintained excellent discipline on capital expenditures. Finally, we are taking steps to drive EBITDA higher through efficiency gains and volume ramps.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Sarah Ellis to discuss our financial results in more detail.

Sarah Ellis: Thank you, John. As John mentioned, we had a strong quarter. Our revenue was $2.1 billion, up 30% year-over-year. Operating income was $850 million, and net income was $620 million. We generated $450 million in free cash flow and returned $150 million to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases. Our balance sheet remains strong, with $3.2 billion in debt and $1.1 billion in cash.

Delving deeper into our adjusted EBITDA, we reported $950 million for the first quarter, representing a 35% increase year-over-year from roughly $700 million in the prior-year period. This marked one of our best quarterly showings in recent years, highlighting the strength of our Permian-focused assets amid steady oil demand and our emphasis on operational efficiencies. Production came in at an average of 245,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, up 15% from last year, led by new wells in the Delaware Basin. Oil specifically averaged around 160,000 barrels per day, a solid gain fueled by extended laterals averaging 12,000 feet and enhanced completion techniques like ceramic proppant pilots that lifted initial rates. Realized pricing supported this, with our blended price at $76 per boe, up from $67 last year—oil fetched $80 per barrel on average, aided by WTI around $81, narrowing differentials, and firm takeaway on pipelines like EPIC and Gray Oak. Gas realizations improved to $3.10 per Mcf alongside Henry Hub strength from LNG exports.

Costs worked in our favor too, with cash operating expenses down 10% to $19 per boe. LOE fell to $8 per boe via AI predictive maintenance across most Permian operations, cutting downtime. G&A dropped to $3 per boe after streamlining our Midland shared services. Regionally, Permian drove over 70% of EBITDA with margins up to 65%, while Eagle Ford held steady despite some deferrals. Hedging at 70% for oil collars around $74-$88 protected gains, and recent acreage adds in Waha bolstered our inventory. We're guiding Q2 EBITDA toward $1.1-$1.2 billion, with Permian activity peaking.

Turning to our midstream segment, which provides stable fee-based cash flows to counter upstream swings, our assets—including over 12,000 miles of pipelines, 50 million barrels of storage, and fractionation in major basins—posted record throughput of 2.5 million boe per day in the quarter, up 15% year-over-year and 5% sequentially. This extends our streak of strong growth, powered by basin production surges and long-term contracts.

Crude volumes led at 1.4 million barrels per day, up 20% year-over-year, with Permian at 1 million barrels per day utilizing expanded lines like Longhorn at over 90%. This cushioned Bakken softness, where tariffs stayed at $3.40 per barrel and 85% of volumes locked in take-or-pay deals akin to our Occidental pacts, shielding from Waha discounts near negative $2 per barrel. Gas transport hit 4.0 Bcf per day, up 10%, spearheaded by Haynesville on Tennessee interconnects, while NGL fractionation reached 300,000 barrels per day with Mont Belvieu ethane strong, pushing EBITDA margins to 60% via plant upgrades. Permian now accounts for 45% of volumes amid high rig activity and consolidations; Eagle Ford and Appalachia added steadily, offset by some Rockies weather impacts hedged at $4.20 per MMBtu.

Segment revenue reached $550 million, up 18% year-over-year, with EBITDA at $360 million and a 65% margin, boosted by 4% tariff hikes on renewals. For infrastructure, we invested $400 million toward our $2 billion annual budget, targeting returns above 12%. Highlights include Phase 2 of Permian Highway with Kinder Morgan at 80% complete, adding compression for Q1 2025 service under MVCs from majors at solid rates; Gulf Coast storage expansions at Nederland hitting high utilization for arbitrage; and a Corpus Christi VLCC port advancing for 2026 amid LNG synergies. Tech like Palantir AI cut leak times 40%, and ESG efforts such as electrified compressors captured 95% methane, supporting sustainability credits. Overall, midstream contributes 40% of EBITDA with 95% fee-based revenues and strong coverage—poised for 12% volume growth next year on a $5 billion project backlog.

On capital expenditures, our full-year guide holds at $1.8-$1.9 billion, with first-quarter spend at $420 million, or 95% of plan, thanks to efficiencies and lower service costs. Drilling was $180 million versus $195 million budgeted, under by 8%, with Permian rigs achieving higher ROP via Halliburton PDC bits extending runs to 6,500 feet and trimming spud-to-TD by over a day. Eagle Ford pad efficiencies and AI geosteering from SLB avoided sidetracks. Completions hit $210 million against $225 million, slightly over at 7% due to high-intensity fracs with SlickFlex designs pumping 1,400 stages, driving 1,700 boe per day IPs in Delaware—Eagle Ford extended laterals helped too. Facilities came in at $30 million under $35 million, deferring tie-ins for electrification at Waha cutting emissions and opex, plus Eagle Ford compression and Bakken water recycling reducing hauls. Total D&C costs dropped 11% to $1.0 million per well, trending us below full-year budget for higher free cash flow at current prices.

I will now turn the call over to Mike Thompson for an operational update.

Mike Thompson: Thank you, Sarah. On the operational front, we continue to execute our strategy effectively. Our production averaged 245,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day. We successfully brought the Thunder Horse South tie-back online in the Gulf of Mexico, which is expected to contribute significantly to our production growth in the coming quarters. We are also making progress on our cost reduction initiatives.

Now I will turn it over to Elena Vasquez for an update on our exploration activities.

Elena Vasquez: Thank you, Mike. We are excited about the potential of our exploration program. We recently completed a successful seismic survey in the Permian Delaware Basin and are planning to drill six exploration wells in the next year. We believe these wells have the potential to add significant reserves to our portfolio.

Operator, we are now ready to open the line for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from John Ramirez with Energy Capital Partners. Please go ahead.

John Ramirez: Thanks, and good morning team. Strong quarter on the production side. Could you walk us through the production guidance for next quarter and the full year, and the key factors driving those projections?

Sarah Ellis: Thanks, John. Happy to dive in. As we outlined in our pre-announce last month, we're guiding for Q2 production of 250,000 to 260,000 boe per day, which represents about a 3% sequential increase from Q1's realized 245,000 boe/d. Oil volumes specifically should come in at 165,000 to 170,000 barrels per day, with natural gas at 500 to 520 MMcf/d and NGLs around 45,000 to 48,000 bbl/d. 

For the full year 2024, we're maintaining our guidance range of 1.05 to 1.10 million boe per day, implying 5% to 8% growth year-over-year from 2023's 1.00 MMboe/d. That breaks down to oil growth of 6% to 9%, gas up 4% to 6%, and NGLs flat to up 2%. This positions us firmly in the upper half of our long-term 5-10% CAGR target through 2027, assuming sustained WTI in the $70-85/bbl range and Henry Hub around $2.75-3.50/MMBtu.

Let me unpack the key factors influencing these projections, starting with the positives driving the upside.

First, operational momentum in the Permian Basin, which accounted for 65% of our Q1 production at roughly 160,000 boe/d. We've ramped our D&C activity to 14 operated rigs—up from 12 in Q4—with two additional rigs sliding into the core Delaware Basin in late Q1. Early results are encouraging: our latest 20-well pad in Loving County posted average IP-30 rates of 2,800 boe/d per well, with 65% oil cut, and lateral lengths averaging 12,500 feet. We're layering in more cube-style developments—think simultaneous fracs across 48+ wells per section—to optimize capital efficiency, targeting sub-$35/boe full-cycle breakevens. This should deliver 15,000-20,000 boe/d of Permian growth for the full year, even as we cycle some Q3 downtime for frac crew rotations.

Second, Eagle Ford optimization is a tailwind, contributing 20% of output at 48,000 boe/d in Q1. Here, we're executing a high-intensity frac program using our proprietary OptiProp proppant blend, which has boosted EURs by 15-20% in recent pilots. We've deferred one rig to Q3 for pad drilling efficiency but expect flat-to-3% growth annually, with richer gas cuts supporting our Karnes County condensate volumes amid strong Gulf Coast LNG demand.

On the offshore Gulf of Mexico side—10% of production at 25,000 boe/d—we brought online the Thunder Horse South tie-back in late Q2 ahead of schedule, adding 5,000 boe/d net at 85% oil. This leverages existing infrastructure from our Thunder Horse field (where we hold a 25% stake alongside BP and Exxon), with low decline curves and $25/boe LOE. We're also progressing four subsea wells at our Mardi Gras JV with Shell, FID expected Q4, which could underpin 10,000+ boe/d ramps in 2025.

Now, factors tempering the guidance and creating the range. Turnaround activity is the biggest near-term headwind: Q2 will see ~10,000 boe/d offline for planned maintenance at our Midland Waha plant (post our $200M expansion last year) and Eagle Ford gas plants, aligning with Kinder Morgan's Whistler pipeline outages. That's baked into the low end of our Q2 guide.

Commodity price sensitivity plays in too. We've hedged 60% of oil volumes at $75/bbl for H2 and 45% of gas at $3.00/MMBtu, but softer Henry Hub forwards—down 15% since January on mild weather and high storage—could pressure realizations if basis weakens further in Appalachia-lite plays. Conversely, Brent-WTI spreads narrowing to $4/bbl supports Gulf of Mexico economics.

Macro and regional headwinds: OPEC+'s extended 2.2 MMbbl/d cuts through Q3 keep a floor under oil, but we're monitoring U.S. rig counts, down 8% YoY per Baker Hughes to 580, signaling basin-wide discipline. Regulatory risks in the Permian—like potential BLM venting/flaring rules—could add $1-2/boe opex, though our 95% capture rate already mitigates that. Internationally, we're pausing North Sea exploration bids amid UK windfall taxes but eyeing Guyana opportunities via Exxon partnerships.

Strategically, this guidance reflects our "efficient growth" playbook: $1.8-1.9B capex skewed 70% to D&C, targeting ROCE >20%. We're prioritizing Tier 1 inventory—3+ years at current pace—with AI-driven geosteering cutting NPT by 25%. Energy transition? We're allocating 5% of capex to CCUS pilots in the Permian, partnering with Occidental on their Stratos project, positioning for 45Q credits while hydrocarbon demand grows 1-2% annually per EIA.

Bottom line, John: This is achievable, disciplined growth with buffers for volatility. We'd need WTI below $60 sustained or major disruptions to hit the low end. Happy to take follow-ups.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from Sarah Jenkins of JPMorgan. Sarah?

Sarah Jenkins: Thanks, and good morning, team. I wanted to dive into your ESG progress, specifically emissions reductions. You've set ambitious targets—can you walk us through the latest on Scope 1 and 2 intensity, methane capture, and how CCUS is scaling? Any regional color or updates on financing?

John Hargrove: Great question, Sarah, and thanks for the focus on ESG—it's core to our value creation strategy at Apex Energy. I'll turn it over to Sarah Ellis, who's been leading our sustainability disclosures, but I'll chime in on the strategic side. Sarah?

Sarah Ellis: Absolutely, John. Good morning, Sarah. We're pleased to report strong progress against our 2030 emissions reduction targets, which align with the Paris Agreement and our SBTi-validated science-based goals: 40-50% absolute reduction in Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions from our 2020 baseline of 15.2 million tCO2e, with net-zero Scope 1 and 2 by 2040 and full net-zero including Scope 3 by 2050. 

Let me break it down with the Q1 numbers. Year-to-date through March, our Scope 1 and 2 emissions totaled roughly 3 million tCO2e, down 25% YoY on a production-adjusted basis—that's against 22 MMboe/d average output. GHG intensity improved to 29 kgCO2e/boe from 36 kg last year and our 2020 baseline of 42 kgCO2e/boe. This puts us on track for 35% reduction by 2025, driven by a multi-pronged approach.

First, methane emissions: We've hit 92% capture rates across our portfolio, reducing intensity to 0.18% of gross gas production—well below the 0.2% target we set with the Oil and Gas Climate Initiative (OGCI). In the Permian, where we operate 1.2 MMboe/d, we've deployed over 2,500 vapor recovery units (VRUs) and continuous monitors, slashing routine flaring by 85% to under 1% of total gas. This mirrors ExxonMobil's Permian success but at lower capex through our modular drone-detection program, which identified 450 high-emitters last quarter alone. Globally, methane down 42% YoY, putting us ahead of EPA's 2024 methane rules.

Flaring's another win: Routine flaring volumes dropped to 0.3 bcf/d, an 82% reduction from 2020, thanks to electrification and gas gathering. In Nigeria's OML 130 block (120 kbopd), we routed 95% of associated gas to our new 200 MMscfd processing train, partnering with Shell for midstream takeaway—avoiding 1.2 million tCO2e annually.

On CCUS, we're accelerating. Our flagship Dorado CCUS hub in the Permian—co-developed with Occidental Petroleum—is capturing 2 MMtpa CO2 from our Waha plant, with Phase 2 FID next quarter at 5 MMtpa. Total capacity will hit 10 MMtpa by 2027, leveraging the IRA's 45Q credits at $85/tonne. We've sequestered 1.5 MMt YTD, offsetting 10% of our Scope 1 footprint. Internationally, in the North Sea's Rosebank field (startup Q4 2025, 300 kbopd), we're integrating ION's Prue Bay storage with 90% CCS readiness, aligning with Norway's 2028 flaring ban.

Electrification is key for Scope 2: 65% of our offshore platforms now run on shore power or hybrid grids, like our Guyana Stabroek block (450 kbopd gross) where Exxon-led FPSO Liza Unity draws from SBM Offshore's 50 MW wind farm. This cut Scope 2 by 35% to 2.1 million tCO2e. We're rolling out Baker Hughes' LM9000 aeroderivative turbines with 40% H2 blending capability across 15 rigs in the Eagle Ford.

Regionally: US onshore (60% of production) leads with 32% intensity reduction, fueled by Permian efficiencies amid WTI at $82/bbl enabling $1.2B green capex. Europe/North Sea (15% portfolio) is at 22% reduction but challenged by higher opex from UK ETS carbon prices at €90/t—yet our Valhall Flank 2 tie-back exceeds 95% uptime with electrification. Emerging basins like Guyana and Namibia (20% growth) start from low baselines but incorporate blue hydrogen pilots; our Venus FPSO design targets 90% methane capture from day one. Middle East JV in ADNOC's Ruwais (100 kbopd) leverages UAE's 100% gas utilization policy, with zero-flaring since 2023.

Trends-wise, per IOGP's 2024 report, industry methane intensity fell to 0.25%, but we're 28% below peers like Chevron. Flaring's down 60% globally per World Bank's data, yet sanctions-hit Russia skews averages—Apex's 0.3% rate positions us top-quartile.

Strategically, these aren't just checkboxes. Emissions cuts drove $250M in avoided methane penalties and carbon credits last year, plus cheaper debt: our green bonds at 3.75% yield versus 4.5% conventional, tapping $15B ESG pools from BlackRock and Temasek. Post-SEC climate disclosure rules (effective 2025), our TCFD-aligned reporting boosts access to EU Taxonomy funding. And with Scope 3 at 450 million tCO2e (mostly combustion), we're collaborating with TotalEnergies on low-carbon fuels—our first 100k bbls of blue diesel shipped Q1.

Forward-looking, we'll invest $4-5B through 2027 on low-carbon tech, targeting 50 kgCO2e/boe intensity by 2030. Risks like supply chain H2 costs or policy shifts (e.g., IRA clawbacks) are mitigated via 20 hedges and OGCI benchmarking. John, over to you on integration.

John Hargrove: Spot on, Sarah. ESG de-risks our 12% IRR portfolio—low-emission barrels command $5-10/bbl premiums in Asia LNG tenders. We're proving oil and gas can decarbonize profitably, creating shareholder value while meeting investor demands for 20-30% emissions cuts. Sarah, happy to follow up post-call.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from John Smith with Energy Capital Partners. Please go ahead.

John Smith: Good morning. Can you elaborate further on the EBITDA drivers this quarter?

Sarah Ellis: Thanks, John. Great question on EBITDA—always the heart of our operational story. As detailed earlier, we delivered adjusted EBITDA of $950 million in Q1 2024, up 35% year-over-year from $700 million in Q1 2023. That's our strongest quarterly performance in some time, underscoring our Permian-centric portfolio amid sustained oil demand and capital efficiency.

Key drivers start with the top line. Production at 245,000 boe/d drove an 18% volume increase year-over-year, with oil at 160,000 bpd up 22%, from 45 new Delaware wells with 12,500-foot laterals and ceramic proppants boosting IPs 15%. Blended realized price at $76/boe, up 14%, with oil at $80/bbl on WTI $81, tight Midland diffs, and gas at $3.10/Mcf from LNG demand.

Costs amplified margins: cash opex down 12% to $18.50/boe, LOE to $7.80 via AI maintenance cutting downtime 30%, transport steady at fixed fees with Enterprise and Targa. G&A to $2.80/boe post-headcount cuts. Permian EBITDA margins hit 68%, Eagle Ford mitigated via hedges, ACG JV steady.

Hedging at 75% collars captured upside, bolt-ons added inventory. Service inflation offset by contracts, royalties up slightly. Q2 guide $1.1-$1.2B with 10% growth potential. John, does that cover it?

Operator: Our next question comes from Laura Chen with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Laura Chen: How will the results of the exploration program affect the company's future strategy?

Elena Vasquez: Thanks, Laura. Our recent Permian seismic and planned six wells build on early successes, potentially adding 50-100 MMboe reserves. This extends our Tier 1 inventory, supporting 5-10% CAGR without higher costs, integrating with CCUS for low-carbon barrels and aligning efficient growth.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. I would like to turn the conference back over to John Hargrove for closing remarks.

John Hargrove: Thank you, Operator. In summary, we are pleased with our performance in the first quarter. We remain focused on executing our strategy and delivering value to our shareholders. Thank you for joining us today.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
